The '''''Zhoubi Suanjing''''',<!--Chinese in infobox; see [[WP:MOS-ZH]]--> also known by [[#Names|many other names]], is an ancient Chinese astronomical and mathematical work. The ''Zhoubi'' is most famous for its presentation of [[Chinese cosmology]] and a form of the [[Pythagorean theorem]]. It claims to present 246 problems worked out by the [[Duke of Zhou]] as well as members of his court, placing its composition during the 11th century&nbsp;BC. However, the present form of the book does not seem to be earlier than the [[Eastern Han]] (25–220&nbsp;AD), with some additions and commentaries continuing to be added for several more centuries.

The book was included as part of the ''[[Ten Computational Canons]]''.

== <span class="anchor" id="Name"></span><span class="anchor" id="Etymology"></span><span class="anchor" id="Translation"></span><span class="anchor" id="Meaning"></span> Names ==
The work's original title was simply the '''''Zhoubi''''': the character {{lang|zh|{{linktext|髀}}}} is a literary term for the [[femur]] or [[thighbone]] but in context only refers to one or more [[gnomon]]s, large sticks whose shadows were used for [[Chinese calendar|Chinese calendrical]] and [[Chinese astronomy|astronomical calculations]].{{sfnp|Needham & al.|1959|p=[https://books.google.com/books?id=jfQ9E0u4pLAC&pg=RA1-PA19 19]}} Because of the ambiguous nature of the character {{lang|zh|{{linktext|周}}}}, it has been alternately understood and translated as 'On the gnomon and the circular paths of [[Tian|Heaven]]',{{sfnp|Needham & al.|1959|p=[https://books.google.com/books?id=jfQ9E0u4pLAC&pg=RA1-PA19 19]}} the 'Zhou shadow gauge manual',{{sfnp|Zou|2011|p=[https://books.google.com/books?id=fD6p-LR_G7UC&pg=PA104 104]}} the 'Gnomon of the Zhou sundial',{{sfnp|Pang-White|2018|p=[https://books.google.com/books?id=EaRTDwAAQBAJ&pg=PT464 464]}} and 'Gnomon of the [[Zhou dynasty]]'.{{sfnp|Cullen|2018|p=[https://books.google.com/books?id=DWV9DwAAQBAJ&pg=PT758 758]}} The honorific '''''Suanjing'''''—'Arithmetical classic',{{sfnp|Needham & al.|1959|p=[https://books.google.com/books?id=jfQ9E0u4pLAC&pg=RA1-PA815 815]}} 'Sacred book of arithmetic',{{sfnp|Davis & al.|1995|p=[https://books.google.com/books?id=I1fj_B60fyoC&pg=PA28 28]}} 'Mathematical canon',{{sfnp|Cullen|2018|p=[https://books.google.com/books?id=DWV9DwAAQBAJ&pg=PT758 758]}} 'Classic of computations',{{sfnp|Elman|2015|p=[https://books.google.com/books?id=lbMyBQAAQBAJ&pg=PA240 240]}}—was added later.

==Dating==
Examples of the [[gnomon]] described in the work have been found from as early as 2300&nbsp;BC and the [[Duke of Zhou]], was an 11th-century&nbsp;BC regent and noble during the first generation of the [[Zhou dynasty]]. The ''Zhoubi'' was traditionally dated to the Duke of Zhou's own life{{sfnp|Needham & al.|1959|p=[https://books.google.com/books?id=jfQ9E0u4pLAC&pg=RA1-PA20 20]}} and considered to be the oldest Chinese mathematical treatise.{{sfnp|Needham & al.|1959|p=[https://books.google.com/books?id=jfQ9E0u4pLAC&pg=RA1-PA19 19]}} However, although some passages seem to come from the [[Warring States period]] or earlier,{{sfnp|Needham & al.|1959|p=[https://books.google.com/books?id=jfQ9E0u4pLAC&pg=RA1-PA20 20]}} the current text of the work mentions [[Lü Buwei]] and is believed to have received its current form no earlier than the [[Eastern Han]], during the 1st or 2nd century. The earliest known mention of the text is from a memorial dedicated to the astronomer [[Cai Yong]] in 178 AD.<ref>{{cite journal
  | last1       = Patrick Morgan
  | first1      = Daniel
  | title       = A Radical Proposition on the Origins of the Received Mathematical Classic The Gnomon of Zhou (Zhoubi 周髀)
  | journal     = The Second International Conference on History of Mathematics and Astronomy
  | date        = 2 November 2018
  | page        = 4
  | url         = https://shs.hal.science/halshs-01900269
  | access-date = 25 December 2023
}}</ref> It does not appear at all in the [[Book of Han]]'s account of calendrical, astronomical, and mathematical works, although [[Joseph Needham]] allows that this may have been from its current contents having previously been provided in several different works listed in the Han history which are otherwise unknown.{{sfnp|Needham & al.|1959|p=[https://books.google.com/books?id=jfQ9E0u4pLAC&pg=RA1-PA19 19]}}

==Contents==
[[File:NAJDA-305-0214 周髀算経 乾.pdf|thumb|page=2|Title page from a Ming dynasty printed edition of the ''Zhoubi Suanjing'']]
[[File:周髀算經.jpg|thumb|Pages of the ''Zhoubi Suanjing'']]
The ''Zhoubi'' is an anonymous collection of 246 problems{{dubious|date=December 2022}} encountered by the Duke of Zhou and figures in his court, including the [[Chinese astrology|astrologer]] Shang Gao. Each problem includes an answer and a corresponding arithmetic [[algorithm]].

It is an important source on early [[Chinese cosmology]], glossing the ancient idea of a round heaven over a square earth ({{lang|zh|{{linktext|天|圆|地|方}}}}, ''tiānyuán dìfāng'') as similar to the round parasol suspended over some ancient [[Chinese chariot]]s{{sfnp|Tseng|2011|pp=45–49}} or a [[Chinese chess]]board.{{sfnp|Ding|2020|p=[https://books.google.com/books?id=kSn_DwAAQBAJ&pg=PA172 172]}} All things measurable were considered variants of the [[square]], while the expansion of a polygon to infinite sides approaches the immeasurable [[circle]].{{sfnp|Zou|2011|p=[https://books.google.com/books?id=fD6p-LR_G7UC&pg=PA104 104]}} This concept of a 'canopy heaven' ({{lang|zh|{{linktext|蓋|天}}}}, ''gàitiān'') had earlier produced the jade [[Bi (jade)|''bi'']] ({{lang|zh|{{linktext|璧}}}}) and [[Cong (vessel)|''cong'']] objects and [[Chinese mythology|myths]] about [[Gonggong]], [[Mount Buzhou]], [[Nüwa]], and [[Nüwa Mends the Heavens|repairing the sky]]. Although this eventually developed into an idea of a 'spherical heaven' ({{lang|zh|{{linktext|渾|天}}}}, ''hùntiān''),{{sfnp|Tseng|2011|p=50}} the ''Zhoubi'' offers numerous explorations of the geometric relationships of simple circles [[Circumscribed quadrilateral|circumscribed by squares]] and squares [[circumscribed circle|circumscribed by circles]].{{sfnp|Tseng|2011|p=51}} A large part of this involves analysis of [[solar declination]] in the Northern Hemisphere at various points throughout the year.{{sfnp|Needham & al.|1959|p=[https://books.google.com/books?id=jfQ9E0u4pLAC&pg=RA1-PA19 19]}}

At one point during its discussion of the shadows cast by gnomons, the work presents a form of the [[Pythagorean theorem]] known as the '''gougu theorem''' ({{lang|zh|{{linktext|勾股|定理}}}}){{sfnp|Cullen|1996|p=82}} from the Chinese names—lit. 'hook' and 'thigh'—of the two sides of the [[carpenter square|carpenter]] or [[try square]].{{sfnp|Gamwell|2016|p=[https://books.google.com/books?id=DfI8CgAAQBAJ&pg=PA39 39]}} In the 3rd century, Zhao Shuang's commentary on the ''Zhoubi'' included a diagram effectively proving the theorem{{sfnp|Cullen|1996|p=208}} for the case of a [[3-4-5 triangle]],{{sfnp|Chemla|2005|p={{page needed|date=October 2020}}}} whence it can be generalized to all [[right triangle]]s. The original text being ambiguous on its own, there is disagreement as to whether this proof was established by Zhao or merely represented an illustration of a previously understood concept earlier than [[Pythagoras]].{{sfnp|Chemla|2005}}{{sfnp|Cullen|1996|p=82}} Shang Gao concludes the gougu problem saying "He who understands the earth is a wise man, and he who understands the heavens is a sage. Knowledge is derived from the shadow [straight line], and the shadow is derived from the gnomon [right angle]. The combination of the gnomon with numbers is what guides and rules the ten thousand things."{{sfnp|Gamwell|2016|p=[https://books.google.com/books?id=DfI8CgAAQBAJ&pg=PA41 41]}}

==Commentaries==
The ''Zhoubi'' has had a prominent place in [[Chinese mathematics]] and was the subject of specific commentaries by Zhao Shuang in the 3rd century, [[Liu Hui]] in 263, by [[Zu Gengzhi]] in the early 6th century, [[Li Chunfeng]] in the 7th century, and [[Yang Hui]] in 1270.

== Translation ==
A translation to English was published in 1996 by Christopher Cullen, through the Cambridge University Press, entitled ''Astronomy and mathematics in ancient China: the Zhou bi suan jing''.<ref>{{Cite book
  | last      = Cullen
  | first     = Christopher
  | title     = Astronomy and mathematics in ancient China: the Zhou bi suan jing
  | date      = 1996
  | publisher = Cambridge University Press
  | isbn      = 978-0-521-55089-5
  | series    = Needham Research Institute studies
  | ref       = none
}}</ref> The work includes a preface attributed to Zhao Shuang, as well as his discussions and diagrams for the gougu theorem, the height of the sun, the seven ''heng'' and his gnomon shadow table, restored.
